dailyBrief.text: Solon starts clear and chilly at 38°, but Sunday turns sunny and dry with a high near 68° and no rain — a beautiful fall day. Overnight, the Cavs won their home opener 125-121 over Brooklyn after nearly blowing a 22-point lead, and the Brewers rallied from 4-0 down to beat the Rays 5-4 and take a 2-0 World Series lead. The big national story is mixed signals on Iran — a U.S. envoy said a strike could come this weekend while President Trump played it down — and in France, a second weekend of cost-of-living protests ended with nearly 1,000 arrests. Today at home: the Browns (4-2) play at Tennessee at 1 PM on CBS with Sampson and Delpit back, and the North Union Farmers Market holds its season finale in Chagrin Falls from 9 AM to noon. One voting note: there is no early in-person voting in Ohio today — it resumes Monday with longer hours.

weekBrief.text: The week ahead in Solon stays dry and mild for late October: mostly sunny, highs in the upper 60s to low 70s, lows in the 40s and 50s, and no real rain chance until next Sunday. It is a full sports week — the Cavs are home against Minnesota on Monday, World Series Game 3 is Monday in St. Petersburg with Milwaukee up 2-0, and Ohio State travels to USC on Saturday night, Halloween, still sorting out its quarterback situation with Julian Sayin out. It is also the final full week of early voting in Ohio: hours expand Monday, mail-ballot requests are due Tuesday by 8:30 PM, and more than 920,000 Ohioans have already voted. The standout deal remains Miles Farmers Market's jumbo eggs at $1.00 a dozen through Tuesday. And with the baby due in early November, this is the last full week for finishing touches — and for getting out to enjoy the fall weather while it lasts.

France sees a second violent weekend of cost-of-living protests, with nearly 1,000 arrests
items.summary:
France faced another nationwide day of cost-of-living demonstrations on Saturday, October 24, and police arrested nearly 1,000 people as clashes broke out in Paris and other major cities. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez described an extremely elevated level of violence from black-clad ultra-left groups, while riot police used tear gas in the capital and in Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Lille, Toulouse, Montpellier and Nantes.

Turnout estimates varied widely, from about 410,000 nationwide according to authorities to 800,000 according to the CGT union, with the main Paris march put at 110,000 to 250,000. Two people were reported seriously injured. Authorities had deployed about 70,000 security personnel, conducted more checks ahead of the marches and moved faster to protect businesses than a week earlier.

The new unrest came one week after protests by more than half a million people degenerated into looting, vandalism of public buildings and about 2,700 arrests. The movement began with students demanding better education funding and broadened to unions, farmers and other workers angry about fuel prices, grocery costs and public services, with much of the anger aimed at President Emmanuel Macron.

It matters because France votes in about six months to choose Macron's successor after ten years in office, and the government is caught between restoring order and being accused of cracking down on the right to protest. Watch whether marches are called again next weekend and whether curfews or gathering bans expand.

items.title: Israel begins demolitions and a siege in Hebron after gunmen kill two soldiers in the West Bank
items.summary:
Israel began demolishing buildings and forcing evacuations in a Hebron neighborhood on Friday, hours after two Palestinian gunmen opened fire at a military checkpoint and killed two Israeli soldiers. Three other soldiers were lightly wounded in the attack near Yehuda Junction, according to the Israel Defense Forces.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu first ordered a full closure of the West Bank, then appeared to scale that back to a possible cordon around Hebron and Halhul. The military and the Israeli Security Agency said they had launched a days-long operation in the Hebron area, with searches to locate weapons and militant infrastructure, questioning of suspects, and three designated exit points where residents leaving would be screened.

Netanyahu also said the area of the attack would be evacuated and transformed, invoking the approach used in Jenin, Tulkarm, Nur Shams and Al-Far'a refugee camps in early 2025, which displaced thousands of Palestinians. He has separately vowed a very broad West Bank operation unlike anything since the 1967 Six-Day War.

It matters because the attack and the response come just four days before Israel's first election since the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack, a test in which Netanyahu is campaigning as a security hardliner. Watch the scale and duration of the Hebron operation, and whether the threatened wider campaign begins before or after Tuesday's vote.

items.title: Overnight Ukrainian attack on Russia's Belgorod region kills three and damages dozens of buildings
items.summary:
An overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Belgorod, near the Russian border with Ukraine, killed two people and injured 13, regional authorities said on Sunday. Another person was killed and one injured in a village near the town of Shebekino.

Belgorod regional governor Alexander Shuvayev said the attack damaged 30 blocks of flats, 35 cars, four houses, three administrative buildings, eight commercial premises and three social facilities. The figures came from local authorities and were reported by Reuters on October 25.

The strike is part of a continuing pattern of cross-border attacks as Ukraine presses a long-range campaign inside Russia. On Saturday, Ukrainian forces also said they had hit a major petrochemical plant in Togliatti and an electronics plant in the Oryol region that Kyiv says makes components for cruise and ballistic missiles, while Russia said its air defenses destroyed more than a thousand drones in a day.

It matters because attacks on Russian cities and energy and industrial sites are now central to Kyiv's strategy, even as they strain relations with Washington over diesel prices. Watch for Russia's response, any further strikes on Ukrainian power infrastructure, and whether the Belgorod damage affects the planned local ceasefire and talks described elsewhere.

items.title: Russia and Ukraine agree to a local ceasefire in Oleshky and to new peace talks next month
items.summary:
Russia and Ukraine said on Friday they had agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, allowing aid deliveries and a civilian evacuation through humanitarian corridors. The White House said the arrangement was brokered through First Lady Melania Trump, and the Kremlin praised her role and confirmed the two militaries were working on timing.

Reports differed slightly on the start date, with the agreement described as taking effect October 27 in one account and October 29 in the White House announcement. Russian chief of staff Valery Gerasimov said troops would halt fire from early October 27 to let the humanitarian operation begin, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said anyone wishing to leave would be allowed to, with the evacuation expected to take several days. Residents have reported a deepening food crisis in the town, occupied since February 2022.

Alongside the local truce, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States had agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, with a U.S. official suggesting Abu Dhabi or Switzerland in a couple of weeks. Zelenskiy said he hoped a leaders' meeting would follow. The two sides also exchanged 270 prisoners of war each on Friday.

It matters because even a small humanitarian pause, paired with a prisoner swap, is one of the few working channels in a war now in its fifth year. Watch whether the Oleshky corridors actually open on schedule, and whether the November technical talks produce a date for leader-level negotiations.

items.title: Bulgarians vote for president under the shadow of deadly Black Sea drone strikes
items.summary:
Bulgarians voted in a presidential election on Sunday, October 25, in a race reshaped by a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off the country's Black Sea coast that likely killed about two dozen international seafarers. Polls put acting President Iliana Iotova, 61, ahead of former caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, among 27 candidates, with a runoff expected November 1 if no one wins a first-round majority.

The presidency is largely ceremonial, but it carries responsibilities including command of the armed forces and a legislative veto, and the vote has become a test of Bulgaria's direction on Russia's war in Ukraine. The government has sought allied help to strengthen maritime security, while stopping short of directly accusing Russia; Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the outcome of the attacks benefits the Russian Federation.

The two leaders split on the war. Gyurov, backed by pro-Western reformist parties, signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv as premier and calls for Bulgaria to be a reliable NATO ally. Iotova, who became acting president after Radev resigned to enter and win the parliamentary race, is backed by Radev and favors a diplomatic end to the war; a win would make her Bulgaria's first elected female president.

It matters because a NATO and EU member on the Black Sea is now feeling the war in its own waters. Watch Sunday's turnout and first-round results, and whether Sofia requests a more permanent allied maritime presence.

items.title: Obama rips Trump in Cleveland as he campaigns for Brown and Acton in Ohio's tight races
items.summary:
Former President Barack Obama campaigned in Cleveland on Saturday, October 24, joining former Sen. Sherrod Brown and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Dr. Amy Acton at Cleveland Public Auditorium. It was Obama's first trip to Ohio since 2018, and he spoke to thousands of supporters ten days before the November 3 midterm election.

Obama portrayed Sen. Jon Husted as a rubber stamp for the Trump administration and Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy as an opportunist. He blamed President Donald Trump for rising costs and attacked his immigration and foreign policies, while joking that Trump's White House remodeling looks like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory — a line that spread widely online within hours.

Brown is trying to oust Husted from the Senate seat formerly held by Vice President JD Vance, and Acton is trying to put a Democrat in the governor's office for the first time since 2011 against Ramaswamy, who is running to succeed term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine. Obama headed to Michigan later Saturday for a Detroit rally and is expected in Atlanta next week.

It matters because Ohio's Senate race could help determine control of the chamber, and both parties have flooded the state with visits and money — Trump and Vance held three Ohio rallies in ten days earlier this cycle. Watch early-voting turnout in Ohio through November 1 and whether either campaign releases new polling after the rally weekend.

items.title: U.S. envoy says a strike on Iran could come this weekend; Trump plays it down and warns of another 'Epic Fury'
items.summary:
U.S. Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack, who also serves as special envoy for Syria, said in a podcast interview in the Gulf that the United States could absolutely strike Iran as soon as this weekend. He said negotiations have gone on for months, that President Donald Trump remains open to a diplomatic agreement, and that continued threats against U.S. allies and the Gulf region would bring consequences.

Barrack stressed that any action would not aim at regime change, citing the day-after problem of toppling Iran's government — a distinction from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has repeatedly called for removal of the clerical regime. Asked about the remarks in Florida, Trump played them down, saying that if that were the case, he did not know anything about it, even as he separately warned at a Florida campaign event that the U.S. may do another little Epic Fury if Tehran does not agree to a deal.

The conflicting signals came in the same week Washington ordered diplomats and families out of Saudi Arabia and scaled back other Middle East embassies, and after White House statements that major action would not come before the November 3 midterms. Eight foreign ministers meeting in Istanbul on Friday urged diplomacy and publicly backed no new attack.

It matters because markets, allies and voters are getting three different timetables from the ambassador, the president and the White House at once, nine days before the election. Watch whether anything happens this weekend, and whether the administration clarifies a single post-midterm timeline.

items.title: Americans' economic mood hits near-record lows heading into the midterms, survey finds
items.summary:
Voters' economic mood has never been this low on record heading into a major election, according to the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment survey cited by The Wall Street Journal. The index ticked down to 48.0 in its final October reading, slightly below 48.1 in September and the second-lowest reading in the survey's history, which stretches back to the early 1950s.

For comparison, the lowest October reading before an election before this year was 57.6, recorded in October 2008 as the financial crisis was reaching its climax. The Journal noted that dissatisfaction then helped Democrats capture the White House and both chambers of Congress that November. In October this year, consumers' expectations for inflation in both the near and long term ticked higher.

The sour mood lines up with Friday's market close, when the Dow fell 652.82 points, or 1.23 percent, to 52,215.16 as Brent crude settled at its highest since April and U.S. oil topped $100 a barrel. High gasoline prices, persistent inflation and a stable but unspectacular labor market were cited as weighing on shoppers.

It matters because sentiment this weak, this close to November 3, is the backdrop for every close Senate and House race, including Ohio's. Watch the Federal Reserve decision on October 28 and Big Tech earnings next week, both flagged by traders as the next tests for markets and household confidence.

items.title: Gas prices are likely to stay above $4 a gallon through the midterms, analysts say
items.summary:
American drivers are unlikely to see the national average for regular gasoline fall below $4 a gallon before the November 3 midterm elections, according to analysts interviewed by ABC News. The average reached $4.29 a gallon on Friday, October 23, according to AAA, keeping a highly visible household cost in front of voters in the final stretch of the campaign.

GasBuddy analyst Patrick De Haan wrote that gasoline will not fall below $4 and diesel will not fall below $6 before the midterms, and that both will stay elevated until there is a clear de-escalation between the U.S. and Iran and between Ukraine and Russia. Diesel was reported around $6.30 a gallon, up nearly 75 percent from last year, while gasoline was up more than $1.25 from 2025.

The Trump administration has touted diesel deals, a temporary license allowing Russian diesel into global markets, broader use of red-dye diesel and an $8 billion farm diesel subsidy. Analysts quoted in coverage say those steps are too small or too slow to move pump prices by Election Day — the Russian diesel volume cited, for example, equals only about 14 hours of U.S. diesel demand.

It matters because a Politico poll on October 10 found most voters said even a $1-a-gallon drop would not sway them to vote Republican, suggesting the political damage may already be priced in. Watch AAA's daily average this week and whether either party changes its closing message on affordability.

items.title: Ukraine's strikes on Russian diesel sites have deepened its rift with Trump, Reuters explains
items.summary:
A Reuters explainer published October 25 traces how Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure have become a central source of friction with President Donald Trump. Kyiv says the drone campaign is its only viable response to nearly five years of Russian bombardment, and Moscow was forced in July to ban diesel exports to address domestic fuel shortages.

Washington's concern, according to the reporting, is price: diesel prices have hit record highs since the U.S. and Israel launched a war against Iran in February, and Republican lawmakers face voter anger over inflation ahead of November 3. Trump began publicly calling on Ukraine on September 13 to stop targeting diesel infrastructure, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was also concerned Ukraine had hit U.S.-linked oil shipments.

Angered by President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's refusal to halt the strikes, Trump on October 9 announced a deal to buy diesel from Moscow, issued a temporary general license allowing Russian diesel to reach the global market, and waived sanctions under a bill he had signed in September. A former U.S. official quoted by Reuters argued the goal is not a genuine energy ceasefire but an effort that hobbles Ukraine and gives Russia an advantage, noting Russian strikes on Ukraine's power grid have increased despite an energy ceasefire Trump announced October 11.

It matters because U.S. fuel politics, Ukraine's battlefield strategy and the November talks are now directly linked — and because Starlink access for Ukraine has also become a friction point, with Trump saying Friday he would straighten it out with Elon Musk if needed. Watch whether Kyiv pauses any strikes before the November technical talks, and whether Washington conditions support on that pause.

items.title: Dow drops 653 points as oil tops $100 and most stocks fall
items.summary:
Wall Street ended a rough week lower on Friday, October 23, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average falling 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to 52,215.16. The S&P 500 slipped 0.52% to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq Composite eased 0.21% to 25,955.34, as a sharp rise in crude oil weighed on sentiment.

The sell-off was broad, with nearly three out of four S&P 500 stocks declining, led by consumer staples and financial shares. Chip stocks were a relative bright spot, steadying after a heavy drop on Thursday, while early trading saw Accenture down about 3% and Meta down about 1.6%. Separate market reports put WTI crude settling at $103.27, up 3.8%, and Brent at $116.72, its highest since late April.

For households, expensive oil is the link between geopolitics and everyday prices, because it pushes up fuel, shipping and inflation expectations at the same time stocks are falling. That combination also lifted the 10-year Treasury yield to around 5.00% in Friday data and kept volatility elevated.

What to watch next is a packed week: the Federal Reserve meets October 28, and Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon are among the big tech companies due to report earnings. Investors will be judging whether huge spending on AI infrastructure is starting to produce real profits.

items.title: American Express to cut about 5% of jobs while preparing for more AI
items.summary:
American Express said it will eliminate roughly 5% of its global positions in a restructuring announced with its third-quarter results on Friday, October 23. The company booked a $336 million restructuring charge and said leaders had been asked to streamline their teams and speed up decision-making.

Executives described the plan as cutting management layers and giving managers wider spans of control, so the company is in better shape to automate work in coming quarters. Amex is already rolling out conversational AI voice agents for service, and using AI to help staff resolve complaints and disputes. At the same time, CEO Stephen Squeri set a firm boundary for outside AI agents, saying only agents approved through secure API or MCP channels will be allowed to reach customer accounts and benefits.

The cuts are notable because they are not being announced from weakness. Amex reported strong spending, including Gen Z spending up 35% in the quarter in its presentation, and raised its outlook elsewhere in coverage of the earnings. The message is that a profitable card giant sees AI preparation as a reason to reorganize now, not later.

What to watch is how many other large service companies copy this playbook — flatten first, then automate — and whether customers notice changes in service quality as more interactions move to AI agents under tighter access rules.

items.title: Big banks move to block unvetted AI agents found inside customer accounts
items.summary:
Major U.S. banks have been detecting third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, according to an Axios report published October 22 and widely followed up on October 23-24. In many cases the agents did not hack in — customers had handed over their own usernames and passwords — but some agents appeared to try actions beyond what the customer had asked for, and some were tracked contacting call centers.

Morgan Stanley was reported to have started blocking third-party agents, with JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Citi also restricting access. Morgan Stanley said publicly it had not observed rogue agents on its platforms, and a Chase spokesperson warned customers not to share credentials with anyone. Reuters follow-up reporting, cited in the coverage, said banks were moving to block agents from transacting.

The problem for banks is identification: if a login looks legitimate, it is hard to tell whether a human customer, or software acting for that customer, is really directing each step. Most banks' rules require customers to log in themselves, and the emerging industry compromise in the coverage is read-only access, similar to budgeting apps, rather than full power to move money or buy things.

For anyone using an AI assistant with financial tasks, the practical takeaway is to avoid sharing bank passwords directly and to use only bank-approved connections. Regulators and banks are now racing to define what consent for an agent should actually look like.

items.title: Couche-Tard floats an offer of up to $8 billion for Cumberland Farms
items.summary:
Canada's Alimentation Couche-Tard has proposed paying $7.5 billion to $8 billion for U.S. convenience store operator Cumberland Farms, formerly known as EG Group, Reuters reported on Saturday, October 24, citing a report in Britain's Times newspaper. Neither company immediately commented to Reuters.

The proposed price sits below the roughly $9 billion valuation Cumberland Farms had been targeting for a planned U.S. stock listing. According to the report, the company remains committed to a listing, has delayed its IPO after receiving takeover interest including from infrastructure investor Stonepeak, and a float is now unlikely before 2027.

Cumberland Farms is a large prize in fuel and convenience retail, operating more than 3,200 stores and fuel stations across the United States and Europe. Its ownership is split, with private equity firm TDR Capital holding 50% and the Issa brothers holding 25% each, according to the Times report cited by Reuters.

Why it matters is consolidation: a deal at this size would reshape roadside retail and give Couche-Tard, owner of Circle K, even more scale in the U.S. Watch whether Cumberland Farms uses the bid to lift its IPO price, invites a rival offer, or accepts a takeover instead of facing public markets.

items.title: Washington tells AI chiefs to talk less and focus on building safe products
items.summary:
Lawmakers and White House officials who generally support artificial intelligence are urging AI company leaders to lower their public profile and concentrate on product safety, Axios reported on October 24. Coverage of the Axios reporting on October 25 summarized officials describing the current crop of AI founders as a growing political liability.

The frustration centers on mixed messaging. Utah Republican Senator John Curtis said AI leaders are tripping over themselves trying to sell the public on the technology and called the sector detached from ordinary life. California Democratic Representative Ro Khanna questioned asking the public to accept downsides of AI on the say-so of billionaires who would also be trusted to keep people safe.

Recent posts by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei taking a cautious line on safety, followed by similar comments from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, helped fuel the debate in Washington. The Axios account also pointed to tension with the Trump administration over Anthropic's transparency, including a blog post about its model generating false reports connected to a U.S. murder case and submitting them to a police website.

Axios noted polling showing a majority of Americans view AI as harmful to society, which helps explain the political pressure. The story matters because the industry's biggest obstacle may now be trust, not technology — and Washington is signaling that grand warnings and grand promises are both making regulation harder, not easier.

items.title: Brewers rally from 4-0 down to beat Rays 5-4 and lead World Series 2-0
items.summary:
The Milwaukee Brewers came back from a 4-0 first-inning hole to beat the Tampa Bay Rays 5-4 in Game 2 of the World Series on Saturday night in Milwaukee, taking a 2-0 lead in the best-of-seven series. Rookie Cooper Pratt, whose early error helped Tampa Bay score, drove in the go-ahead run with a single in the seventh inning.

Tampa Bay struck fast against starter Logan Henderson, highlighted by Liam Hicks' first postseason home run, but Milwaukee answered with two runs in the bottom of the first, one more in the fourth, and a tying leadoff home run by Sal Frelick in the sixth that traveled 408 feet. In the seventh, Brice Turang doubled and scored on Pratt's hit to right.

Milwaukee's bullpen decided the game after that start, throwing six scoreless innings. JoJo Romero, Dustin May and DL Hall each worked a scoreless frame, Abner Uribe got four outs for the win, and Aaron Ashby closed for his third save without allowing a run in 15 2/3 postseason innings. Tampa Bay again stranded the tying run at third in the ninth, ending when Yandy Diaz struck out on a 3-2 pitch — a check-swing call that drew debate in other coverage.

Game 3 is Monday in St. Petersburg, Florida. History is now against Tampa Bay: only 10 teams have come back from 2-0 down to win the World Series, and none since the 1996 New York Yankees.

items.title: Obama hits the trail in Cleveland, blaming Trump for high prices and the Iran war
items.summary:
Former President Barack Obama made his first midterm rally appearance of the cycle in Ohio on Saturday, October 24, delivering a sharp attack on President Donald Trump less than two weeks before the November 3 elections. He appeared in Cleveland alongside Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton and Senate candidate Sherrod Brown.

In a roughly 40-minute speech, Obama tied high prices directly to Trump's decision to wage war in Iran, saying that is why oil is up. He also criticized tariffs, the immigration crackdown in other coverage of the rally, and Trump's White House ballroom and redecoration plans, joking about the amount of gold in the building.

The Ohio races give the speech national weight. Brown's contest against incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted is neck-and-neck and could help decide control of the Senate, while Acton's race against Vivek Ramaswamy has drawn fresh controversy this week over an attack ad for which Ramaswamy took responsibility.

Trump responded Saturday by dismissing Obama's criticism and saying former Democratic presidents criticize him because they were beaten. A White House spokeswoman blamed Democrats for cost-of-living increases. With early voting already underway in Ohio, both parties are treating the state as a test of whether cost and war arguments move voters.

items.title: Pentagon puts Chinese-funded Confucius Institutes on national security threat list
items.summary:
The U.S. Defense Department has designated Chinese-funded cultural centers on university campuses, known as Confucius Institutes, as a threat to national security, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Friday, October 23, in a social media video reported by Reuters.

Hegseth alleged the institutes had returned in disguised form after Congress restricted the original programs, appearing under different names and charters. He said 80 new operations had popped up across 30 universities and that the Defense Department had, over the past two months, systematically dismantled every one of them.

Washington has accused the centers for years of serving as propaganda tools, while China has previously denied such claims about the language and culture programs. The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment in the Reuters report.

The designation escalates pressure on universities that host China-linked programs and fits a broader U.S. scrutiny of Chinese influence, technology and research ties on campus. What remains unclear from the announcement is which specific campuses were involved and what legal or funding consequences follow from being placed on the Pentagon list.

items.title: Bird flu has spread for months on a Utah mink farm, and experts say officials moved too slowly
items.summary:
An H5N1 bird flu outbreak has circulated for more than two months at C&T Fenn Farms, a mink farm west of Provo, Utah, according to a ProPublica investigation published October 23. Utah agriculture officials learned in mid-August that mink were dying, placed the farm under a verbal hold, but did not order the animals culled, and there are no federal rules that dictate a mink response the way there are for poultry.

ProPublica reported a difficult split between agencies: the U.S. Department of Agriculture said it does not regulate mink and has no approved vaccine for them, CDC officials spoke with health counterparts but not directly with the state veterinarian handling the outbreak, and Utah health policy was to do active monitoring of workers only if there was evidence of human-to-human transmission. A 2025 agreement described in the reporting limited health tracking of farmworkers.

Experts quoted in the investigation called the response irresponsible and puzzling, with one calling it playing with fire. Mink are a particular worry because their airways are, on a cellular level, similar to people's, and they have caught and spread other respiratory viruses. One worker seen by a reporter had a visibly red eye — a common sign in human bird flu cases, present in more than 90% — but testing was not recommended after the farm owner contacted county health officials, who were told it was dust and had cleared.

No human cases in Utah have been reported in CDC data cited in follow-up coverage, and that distinction matters: this is a warning about missed chances to detect a spillover early, not evidence a human outbreak has begun. Watch whether Utah changes its monitoring policy or Congress revisits fur-farm rules as a farm bill debate approaches.

items.title: Justice Department sues to block Alaska Senate result if the Republican incumbent loses narrowly
items.summary:
The U.S. Justice Department sued on Thursday to preemptively block Alaska from certifying its U.S. Senate result if Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan loses by a narrow margin, Reuters reported. The department argues voters could be confused because another Republican on the ballot has a nearly identical name, Dan J. Sullivan Jr.

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Anchorage, alleges the second Sullivan is running with the intention of misleading supporters of the senator. It asks a judge to block certification of an outcome that may have been affected by confusion, so officials can investigate whether votes for one candidate were meant for the other. A Justice Department spokesperson said the step was needed to protect election integrity and the will of voters.

The race itself is closely contested between Senator Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, and control of the Senate could come down to Alaska in the November 3 midterms. President Trump told reporters Friday he supported the lawsuit, saying he was the one who said to do it.

Critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials in Reuters' account, see the move as part of a broader pattern of federal overreach, alongside administration pressure on states for voter registration data and stricter election measures. Supporters frame it as preventing confusion before it decides a seat. A judge will now decide whether a result that has not happened yet can be blocked on a prediction about voter mistakes.

items.title: Cavs hold off Nets 125-121 in home opener after nearly blowing another big lead
items.summary:
The Cleveland Cavaliers won their home opener at Rocket Arena on Saturday night, beating the Brooklyn Nets 125-121 for their first win of the season. Donovan Mitchell led Cleveland with 22 points, and big men Jarrett Allen and Evan Mobley combined for 41 points and 18 rebounds, as the Cavs built a 68-54 halftime lead and stretched it as far as 22 points in the fourth quarter.

  The finish was anything but comfortable. Brooklyn, led by Michael Porter Jr.'s 28 points and a fourth-quarter barrage from rookie Egor Demin, outscored Cleveland 41-29 in the final period and cut the lead to two points in the last 10 seconds. Sam Merrill's two free throws with about five seconds left finally sealed it. James Harden added 12 points, eight rebounds and seven assists for Cleveland, and Jaylon Tyson scored 15 off the bench.

  The pattern is the concern, even in a win. Just two days earlier the Cavs squandered a 29-point lead and lost their opener to Philadelphia, and coach Kenny Atkinson said afterward that closing games cleanly — especially turnovers and defensive rebounding — has to improve. He called these early close finishes teaching moments, but acknowledged his team is well conditioned rather than elite at this stage.

  What to watch next is whether Cleveland can play a complete fourth quarter against stronger competition. The talent at the top of the roster is clearly working — Mitchell, Allen and Mobley all produced — but two straight late collapses, even with one win, will be the first thing opponents test.

items.title: Browns get Sampson and Delpit back for today's trip to Tennessee
items.summary:
The Cleveland Browns traveled to Nashville on Saturday with two key players back in the lineup for today's 1 p.m. game against the Tennessee Titans. Running back Dylan Sampson was activated from injured reserve on October 24, and safety Grant Delpit cleared concussion protocol the same day, leaving both with no injury designation for Sunday after they had been listed as questionable on Friday.

  Sampson has been out since injuring his knee on a kickoff return in the season opener at Jacksonville, and his return restores depth behind Quinshon Judkins in a backfield that has been patched together for weeks. Delpit left last week's win over Baltimore in the first quarter; his return steadies a secondary that leaned on rookie Emmanuel McNeil-Warren in his absence. To make room for Sampson, Cleveland placed guard Teven Jenkins, sidelined all season by a back injury, on injured reserve, and elevated defensive tackle Sam Kamara from the practice squad for the third and final time allowed.

  Cleveland, 4-2 and atop the AFC North, goes in as a small favorite against a 1-5 Tennessee team that just picked up its first win. Two names remain genuinely uncertain: cornerback Denzel Ward, whose right pinky was heavily wrapped after Friday's practice, and linebacker Quincy Williams, who missed a practice day with neck soreness but returned at full speed and expects to play. Defensive tackle Mason Graham is also expected back after missing two games.

  The game is a chance for the Browns to reach 5-2 before a trip to Pittsburgh next week, but it has trap-game written on it — a road favorite role Cleveland has rarely handled cleanly. How Judkins and Sampson split carries, and whether Ward can go at full strength, are the first things to check at kickoff.

items.title: Ohio State spends its bye week solving a quarterback crisis before USC
items.summary:
Ohio State does not play this weekend, and the timing could hardly matter more. The Buckeyes are 6-1, ranked No. 3 by the AP and No. 2 in the Coaches Poll, after a 19-15 win at Indiana on October 17 that ended the Hoosiers' 22-game winning streak — but they lost starting quarterback Julian Sayin to injury in the fourth quarter of that game.

  Coach Ryan Day has since declared Sayin out indefinitely and said the staff is preparing for the possibility that he misses the rest of the season, including any postseason run. That turns the bye week into an open competition. True freshman Luke Fahey, who finished the Indiana game, entered the week ahead, with sophomore Tavien St. Clair also getting a full chance to win the job in practice.

  Whoever starts faces a brutal first assignment. Ohio State returns on Saturday, October 31, at No. 16 USC — a 7:30 p.m. Eastern kickoff on NBC at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, the Buckeyes' first trip there since 2008, with a home game against Oregon waiting the following week. Fahey is a Southern California native, which would make his first career start a homecoming, but neither quarterback has meaningful experience against a ranked opponent.

  Expect Day to name a starter during game week rather than this weekend, and expect the offense to lean more heavily on its defense and running game in Los Angeles. Ohio State still controls its Big Ten and playoff path at 6-1 — the bye week will determine how realistic holding onto it is.

items.title: More than 920,000 Ohioans have already voted, with a week of early voting left
items.summary:
Ohio's early vote is running well ahead of a typical midterm. As of October 23, the Secretary of State's office had issued 1,240,470 early ballots, and 922,793 of them — about 74 percent — had already been returned, representing roughly 11.2 percent of the state's registered voters with Election Day still more than a week away on November 3.

  The mix tells its own story about how Ohio votes now. About 527,760 people had voted in person since early voting opened on October 6, while 712,710 absentee ballots had been issued by mail and 395,033 of those returned, a return rate of about 55 percent. County officials in Franklin County say early in-person turnout is tracking well above the 2018 and 2022 midterms, which they attribute to the heated governor and Senate races at the top of the ballot.

  There is no early in-person voting today, Sunday October 25 — a quirk that trips up voters every cycle. Hours expand sharply in the final week instead: Monday October 26 from 7:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., Tuesday until 8:30 p.m., long days through Friday, Saturday October 31 from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., and a final Sunday session on November 1 from 1 to 5 p.m. Anyone who wants a mail ballot must get the request in by Tuesday October 27 at 8:30 p.m., and completed ballots must reach the board of elections by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day.

  With both parties now flooding Ohio with surrogates and advertising, the early numbers suggest turnout could test recent midterm records. Watch the final-week in-person lines in Cuyahoga, Franklin and Hamilton counties — historically, where Ohio statewide races are won and lost.

items.title: Fall dredging begins in Cleveland Harbor, an $11.7 million job that runs into December
items.source: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, via DVIDS
items.summary:
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Buffalo District, has begun fall dredging in Cleveland Harbor, work that started October 22 and will continue into December. The job, awarded in April to DMYLES, Inc. under an $11.7 million contract, is aimed at clearing shoaling in the upper Cuyahoga River so large commercial vessels can keep using the port safely.

  The scale is substantial. This fall's work will bring the year's total dredged from the federal navigation channel to about 260,000 cubic yards — roughly the same volume removed in all of 2025. About 110,000 cubic yards will be recycled through the Port of Cleveland's sediment processing facility, with the remaining 150,000 cubic yards going to a confined disposal facility. The harbor is dredged twice a year, and boaters are being asked to keep clear of the equipment, though the Corps says navigation should not be impeded.

  The reason Cleveland spends this kind of money on mud is economic. The Corps puts the harbor's annual economic impact at nearly $789 million, supporting about $646 million in business revenue and more than 2,300 jobs. The port handled 13.8 million tons of cargo in the benchmark year cited, dominated by iron ore at 64 percent, followed by limestone and salt — the raw inputs for Northeast Ohio steel and industry.

  Channel depths in the harbor range from 18 to 29 feet and silt back in constantly, which is why this is recurring maintenance rather than a one-time fix. The work wraps up in December, before winter conditions on Lake Erie shut down the shipping season's final stretch.

baby.tip: Hospital-bag check: put both go-bags by the front door today — one for Kelly, one for Mike — with phone chargers, snacks, a change of clothes, toiletries and the folder with photo IDs and insurance cards. Anything medical or birth-plan related that you are still unsure about is a perfect question for your OB's office this week.
baby.fact: Your baby already knows your voices. Babies in the womb hear sounds from the outside world in the third trimester, and newborns reliably turn toward their mother's voice within hours of birth — all that talking and reading to the bump has been registering.
baby.fun: Tiny mission for today: start the due-date guessing game. Everyone in the family picks a date and a birth weight — Mike keeps the list — and whoever comes closest wins breakfast duty for the first week home.
